commit.message:
[datakit] Key quality scores by scorer identity and rescore the corpus

The quality score path derived from the tokenize leaf, so the scorer never
appeared in it: two pins over one tokenization resolved to the same directory,
and a step could claim one model while reading another's bytes. `quality()` is
now an ordinary step whose output sits at `name_with_hash`. The model and
calibration digests go in `hash_attrs` and the tokenization enters through
`dep_names`, because `tokenized()` is a dependency rather than a leaf name
spliced into a string, so a pin that differs anywhere gives a different path.

With one complete Harrier leaf per source (#8270) the whole corpus is scorable,
so all 292 sources were rescored into that layout: 18,710,478,349 documents over
162,535 shards in 3h15m on 6x8 H100. Scored rows equal embed rows equal the sum
of normalize's counters exactly, with no shard left unmatched. Sampling 634,006
rows against the previously written dataset reproduced every score bit for bit,
against a 5.19e-4 tolerance that exists for GPU-vs-CPU reduction ordering. The
old dataset at `datakit/quality-scores/` is untouched.

The join emits exactly one row per embed row. It was driven from the token side,
where `searchsorted` takes a single match, so a repeated id on the embed side
scored only its first row and lost the rest, while a repeated id on the token
side scored the same embed row twice; with duplicates on both sides the match
took their cross product, turning 6,095 embed rows into 6,331 on one shard. It
is now driven from the embed side, with the token side collapsed to one row per
distinct id and each id claiming its whole run of embed rows exactly once, and
each shard asserts its output cardinality rather than assuming it.

Duplicate ids are preserved and reported rather than deduplicated. A duplicate
id is byte-identical text, so it has identical tokens and an identical score,
and dropping one would lose the row-for-row correspondence with the token store
that is the harder property to recover downstream.

The manifest refuses to build for any source whose token and embed sides share
no shard basename. That state is invisible to row counts and artifact metadata,
and it is what a normalize rerun on one side produces: the documents would
otherwise land in an unembedded counter that reads as coverage.

Bulk reads retry with jittered exponential backoff. CoreWeave severs connections
mid-body at roughly one per minute against a single leaf, with no size
selectivity, and unretried over 162,535 shards that becomes a task failure
indistinguishable from a real data fault. A shard is the retry unit, because the
token stream cannot resume mid-body without re-emitting blocks that were already
scored, so a restart discards the shard's partial state.

commit.message:
[datakit] Check the scorer's bytes and the shard pairing before writing

The output path folds in `model_sha256`, so scores written under it claim to be
that model's, but `--model-dir` was a free argument and nothing compared the two.
`score` now digests the directory it is about to load and refuses to run unless it
matches the pin, once at process start rather than per shard. The digest is the
recipe `QualityPin` documents, now runnable as `score_corpus digest`; over the
deployed folded directory it reproduces e1be09c9, so the check passes for the run
already on disk. `--model-tag` is gone for the same reason: it let the `model`
column disagree with the bytes that produced the scores.

The manifest compared the two leaves' shard basenames only for total disjointness.
A partial overlap passed, and since rows are enumerated from the token side, an
embed shard the token side does not name never becomes a row: its documents miss
the manifest, the footer totals, scoring and verification together, leaving every
remaining count self-consistent. The guard now runs on the complete basename sets.
The completed run had no such shard -- summed embed rows equal normalize's counters
exactly for all 292 sources, which they could not if an embed shard were missing --
so this changes nothing for that input.

A shard whose embed rows the token side did not carry warned and then wrote the
matched subset, so the worker exited zero having published a short shard. It raises
now, before the write.

Reading extremes let a missing normalized text shard become a skipped shard and a
smaller reported count; it propagates. `--shards-per-source` selected one shard from
each of N sources, never N shards, and is named `--sources-per-pattern` for what it
does.

commit.message:
datakit: add the hero store entry point

Build the final (cluster x quality) store from the stages hero_data names,
rather than by walking the reference DAG. StepRunner gets one terminal and
every dependency is a read-only hero step, so no upstream stage is rebuilt.

The store now cuts the quality score itself. score_corpus writes narrow
id/score shards and no bucket column, so build_clustered_store takes the score
directory plus the cutpoints instead of a QualityScores artifact, and digitizes
at read time. The cutpoints are the calibration's interior knots, which is the
same partition as calibrating first and cutting at BUCKET_EDGES.

hero_data gains decontam and verified_fuzzy_dups. Decontamination is pinned per
source like harrier, because its step folds in an eval bloom and a drop-set
stage that have both moved since the run: rebuilding it from current code
resolves to a directory nothing wrote. Both stages raise PendingRegistration
until their producing job lands, and --pending reports them together.

--preflight replays the store's own checks for a few thousand small reads and
no cluster time, and adds one the store cannot make: duplicate attributes are
sparse, so a dedup directory built against an older normalize of a source reads
as "no duplicates" rather than as an error.

commit.message:
datakit: repack the focus crawl's exact-duplicate marks

Both pinned dedup runs read the focus crawl's jusText extraction, before #8111
sent that tree through normalize_step, so their marks are addressed by shard
names the current source does not use. Fuzzy verification repacks its own
candidates; the exact marks had no such pass, and duplicate attributes are
sparse, so the store reads the mismatch as "no duplicates" rather than as an
error and the source keeps every exact duplicate it has.

Renaming shards is not enough. The extraction held 12.2% duplicate rows and
normalize_step defaults to DedupMode.EXACT, so each id now appears once, and a
mark written against a copy that normalize removed would delete the copy that
remains. Counting settles which marks still apply: global exact dedup keeps one
occurrence of an id, so a source with f occurrences and f-1 marks held the
canonical copy and must keep it, while one with f marks was a duplicate of
another source and still is. Reading the extraction's id column is what makes f
available, which is why this repack reads the old source and the fuzzy one does
not.

produce_store runs the repack ahead of the store and reads its output instead of
the pin. Preflight reads the pin, since the repack is the one input that does
not exist until the run produces it, and checks that the pin still holds the
legacy key and not the current one.

datakit: count the marks the exact repack keeps and drops

every id is what normalize already reported as duplicate_records_out,

documents duplicate something outside it. marks_kept must come out at 3, and a
rename would have carried all 14,316,837 across and deleted 65.0% of the
22,010,234 documents the source has left.

Also corrects the duplicate share in the module docstring. It cited the 12.2%
that #8111 measured on a 24-shard sample; over the whole source normalize
removed 14,316,834 of 36,327,068 rows, which is 39.4%.

commit.message:
datakit: allow the exact repack to run ahead of the store

The repack reads the pinned dedup run and the focus crawl's normalize, neither of
which the store is waiting on, so it can run before decontamination and quality
are registered. --repack-only builds it through the same call store_inputs
makes, so it lands at the identity the store will depend on and is served from
cache rather than run twice.

Running it early is how marks_kept gets checked while there is still time to act
on it. The store run would otherwise be the first thing to exercise a shuffle
over 36.3M ids across 4,573 shards.

commit.message:
datakit: walk the decon tree instead of globbing it

Discovery globbed datakit/decontam/ at three depths to find <source>_<hash>
directories. A glob deep enough to reach the third level enumerates every
Parquet shard under all of them, which is millions of keys to answer a question
about directory names, and it does not return in any useful time. It now lists
one delimited level at a time and descends only into prefixes a registered
source name actually starts with.

Leaf detection reads the artifact file rather than the name. finepdfs is a
registered source and the parent of eighteen more, so the run writes both
finepdfs_<hash> and finepdfs/<lang>_<hash>; a name test matches the bare parent,
records it as the source, and never descends, which lost all eighteen. Against
datakit/quality, which nests the same way and is complete, the walk now resolves
292 of 292 in 19s.

commit.message:
datakit: drop the decontamination discovery script

Searching storage for a stage's directory is not something this pipeline should
do. Every other hero stage is either recomputed from code or recorded as a path,
and decontamination is recorded, so the map is the registration -- there is
nothing to find.

The script existed on a false premise of mine: the decon hash is not
reproducible from main, from which I concluded it had to be discovered. It is
reproducible from the code that produced it, so the run that writes the data
records its own paths, the way the Harrier map was recorded.

Searching also cost a real bug. finepdfs is a registered source and the parent of
eighteen more, so a name test matched the bare parent directory and lost all
eighteen from the map.

commit.message:
datakit: check the calibration against its pin before reading cutpoints

The path to the calibration is a constant copied from an argparse default, and
nothing compared it against calibration_sha256. That is the collision #8303
closed on the model side, reopened on the read side: the cutpoints decide which
bucket every document in the corpus lands in, and they were taken from whatever
file the constant happened to name.

Verified against storage: the file digests to the pinned 1a1dcfd3, and the folded
model directory to the pinned e1be09c9, so the constant is right today. The check
is what keeps it right.

Also corrects the pin's docstring. calibration_sha256 is the plain SHA-256 of the
file, not the path-folded recipe model_sha256 uses; that recipe gives b89b7b78.
The file sits inside the model directory, so model_sha256 already covers it.

commit.message:
datakit: cut quality buckets at the content type's own calibration

The calibration ships a fitted set of cutpoints for each of six content types
and nothing read them. Measured on this corpus, cutting at the content-blind
default instead moves 36% of math documents and 24% of code documents into a
different bucket, consistently a higher one: math's top bucket goes from 465,759
to 322,047 documents, code's from 12,662 to 8,257.

The store now reads the per-document content type alongside the score and
digitizes each row against its own type's knots, one digitize per distinct type
per shard rather than per row. A type with no calibration falls to default,
which covers `other` and anything the classifier emits later, and those rows are
counted so the fallback cannot be silent. The content-type column joins the
strict id-alignment check, because a misaligned one buckets documents under
another kind of content rather than failing.

ClusteredStoreData records cutpoints per type, so its bucket_edges becomes a
mapping and the artifact goes to v5. The reference pipeline has no content-type
stage and passes default alone.

commit.message:
datakit: size the store's local disk from the measured corpus

A task spills every surviving token of every shard it owns to /tmp, which on
Kubernetes is a disk-backed emptyDir under the pod's ephemeral-storage limit.
Exceeding it is a kubelet eviction, and enough evictions trip max_task_failures
and take the whole gang down rather than one task. That is how a 3-source run
died at 64 GiB per task.

Measured from the tokenize footers rather than assumed: the registered corpus is
26.1 T tokens, 95.1 TiB of int32 spill over 162,535 shards. The previous default
of 192 tasks averages 507 GiB against a 900 GiB disk, which fits the mean and
not the spread -- shards are dealt round robin but stack-v3 alone is 13.5 TiB
and finetranslations 10.3 TiB, so a task drawing from the dense end runs well
above average, and the estimate excludes the per-run length files.

384 tasks at 1200 GiB puts the mean at 254 GiB, about 4.7x headroom, and halves
each task's wall time. Disk carries most of the change because task_count is not
free: every task writes its own cache per populated bucket before the ledgers
merge, and a 3-source run at 128 tasks already wrote 25,432 caches for 200 final
buckets.

1200 GiB is 4.4% of a node's 26.5 TiB, so the pod still packs and does not
become a near-whole-node gang that Kueue declines to admit.

commit.message:
datakit: record what each source contributed to the store

Every counter the store emits is a corpus-wide total. Over 292 sources that
cannot answer the question worth asking -- did each one contribute what it
should -- because a source that joined to nothing, or to far too much,
disappears into the aggregate.

ClusteredStoreData now carries a SourceStats per source: records in and out,
tokens out, and what each of the three filters took. These are the numbers
_FilterStats already computes per shard, and a shard belongs to exactly one
source, so this is a roll-up rather than a second measurement. It rides the path
that already carries the corpus counters out of the spawned join processes --
returned as data, rolled up per task, written to the sidecar, merged by the
driver -- rather than a new channel, which is what keeps a subprocess from
counting into a store the parent never reads.

When every task reports per-source totals, a source absent from the merge fails
the run. The check is skipped when any task does not, because a run resumed
across this change reads sidecars written before it, and failing on those would
break the retry path the sidecars exist for.

commit.message:
datakit: audit whether a tokenization is one row per document

The store tells "one document across three rows" from "three documents" by
chunk_index, and refuses a leaf that lacks the column rather than risk a silent
misalignment after the first oversized document. The Marin fleet run predates
#8100 and has no such column, so it is refused.

That refusal is right for a leaf that might be chunked and cannot say so, and
unnecessary for one that provably is not. A document spanning rows makes its
shard hold more rows than the source has documents, so comparing every shard
against the decontamination side decides it. Sampling cannot: a single chunked
shard among 162,535 is exactly what hides.

Runs as a Zephyr job with 400 shards per task, reading footers only.

commit.message:
[datakit] Drop fuzzy duplicates at 0.60 word 3-gram containment

The verifier required containment of exactly 1.0 plus zero novel word 8-grams.
Nothing it accepted was wrong, and it accepted almost nothing: against 312
candidate pairs labeled blind across five content types it found 11.3% of the
true duplicates, and on math and instruction data it found none at all, so
those sources were never deduplicated in practice.

A near-duplicate survives light editing, but every edit destroys the n-grams
spanning it, so a threshold near 1.0 rejects genuine duplicates. Verified
duplicates sit between 0.62 and 0.81 containment while pairs that connected
components merged by transitive closure sit near 0. At 0.60 the rule keeps
87.7% of true duplicates and 1.5% of what it accepts is a genuinely different
document, almost all of it one shape: a shared template carrying different
values, such as a multiple-choice item repeated with different options.

The zero-novel-token clause is deleted rather than kept. At the new threshold it
admitted no pair the containment gate had not already taken, so it was a second
code path and a second parameter for no behavioral difference.

Length ratio, a numeric-token veto, and containment measured on n-grams
discounted by cluster document frequency were each tested and rejected. The
length guard fires on 0.01% of pairs; the numeric veto refuses 59.8% of
near-certain code duplicates, whose line numbers and version strings differ; and
discounting cluster-common n-grams destroys the signal, because in a cluster of
duplicates the shared text is the evidence.

The module had no test coverage. It now has tests for the threshold boundary,
order independence, subset removal, and agreement between the exact-scan and
inverted-index paths.

[datakit] Route cluster groups through a wider key space

The grouping key was already a shard index in [0, output_shards), and zephyr

serves that text from worker memory stores on every run, so each rule change

validator requires exactly one description, because an artifact that does not
say which rule deleted a document cannot be audited afterwards. Consumers read

commit.message:
[datakit] Price several containment thresholds in one verification pass

Choosing a duplicate threshold meant running the verifier once per candidate
value, and each run reads the whole 17.7 TiB cluster-text dataset and shuffles
its markers. Building the n-gram sets dominates that cost and does not depend on
the threshold, so one prepare now feeds a cover per threshold. Measured on real
clusters a cover is 15% of a single-threshold solve against 51% for the n-gram
build, so four thresholds cost about 45% more than one rather than 300% more.

Each threshold gets its own ordinary marker tree under markers@<t>, with its own
source manifest and artifact, so choosing one is repointing a path and the store
is unchanged. The map emits one record per removed document carrying a bitmask of
the thresholds that removed it, and the reduce expands the mask on the write
side, which keeps the shuffle at a single threshold's size. The mask is not part
of the marker schema and never reaches a written tree.

The mask cannot collapse to the strictest threshold that fired, because removal
is not monotonic: lowering the bar can absorb a member's only representative and
let the member survive. A cluster was measured dropping a document at 0.50 and
keeping it at 0.45 for exactly that reason.

Each tree also carries a SUCCESS status file. A pinned dependency is pruned from
the schedule only when its output has one, and hero_data pins a verified-duplicate
tree with a step whose fn raises if anything runs it, so without the marker the
store would fail at scheduling rather than on the data. A hand run has no executor
to write it; a run through cluster_verify_step gets the real one.

commit.message:
[datakit] Give cluster verification a retry budget the reduce can use

The first production run aborted after the reduce had written markers for
153 of 292 sources. Seven reduce shards of 2,048 hit Zephyr's default of
three attempts, each failing on
EndpointConnectionError against marin-us-east-02a.cwlota.com.

Three strikes is the wrong budget for this stage. One reduce attempt
opens every mapper's chunk, so the wave issues roughly 13 million
object-store requests, and a brief endpoint outage lands on many shards
at once rather than singling out a bad one. Botocore already retries five
times per request underneath, so a shard that burns an attempt has hit an
outage longer than that, not a defect in its data.

Aborting is expensive because Zephyr deletes the scatter tree on abort:
the run loses the whole map stage, which was two hours here, and cannot
resume. Default to 20 attempts and expose the knob.

commit.message:
[zephyr] Retry the shuffle sidecar read on a transient object-store error

A reducer reads one metadata.msgpack per mapper before it can build its
ScatterReader, so a shard with thousands of mappers was one bad GET away
from losing the whole scan. EndpointConnectionError subclasses
botocore's ConnectionError rather than HTTPClientError, so it is absent
from s3fs's S3_RETRYABLE_ERRORS and s3fs gives up at the first
occurrence. What remained was botocore's own five attempts, which cover
about 15 seconds and draw on a per-client quota that 32 concurrent
readers can drain during a single outage.

Wrap the read in retry_with_backoff with is_transient_s3_error, the same
pairing atomic.py and fsutil/listing.py already use, and name the
sidecar when the read cannot recover -- the bare decode error did not
say which sidecar it came from.

Fixes #8389

_SIDECAR_READ_CONCURRENCY is per task, and a wave is thousands of tasks, so
the product is what the object store sees. At 32 a 2,048-reducer wave offers

closer to 105,000.

reading a sidecar and on "error sending request" reading a Parquet footer.
Both are connection-level failures rather than throttle responses or 503s,
which is what a refused connection looks like rather than a rejected request.
The retries added at the s3fs, botocore and Polars object_store layers all
treat the symptom; none of them reduce the offered load.

Drop it to 8. The pool still hides read latency, and the peak falls fourfold.

[zephyr] Cut the scatter read pool so a reduce wave stops refusing connections

_SIDECAR_READ_CONCURRENCY is per task, and a wave is thousands of tasks, so
the product is what the object store sees. At 32 a 2,048-reducer wave offers
roughly 65,000 simultaneous connections, and the larger production runs offered
closer to 105,000.

Fuzzy verification died three times against that, on EndpointConnectionError
reading a sidecar and on "error sending request" reading a Parquet footer.
Both are connection-level failures rather than throttle responses or 503s,
which is what a refused connection looks like rather than a rejected request.
The retries added at the s3fs, botocore and Polars object_store layers all
treat the symptom; none of them reduce the offered load.

Drop it to 8. The pool still hides read latency, and the peak falls fourfold.

commit.message:
[zephyr] Retry the shared-data read that every task in a wave makes at once

get_shared fetches one object key, and every task in a stage fetches the same
one at startup, so the herd is as wide as the fan-out. Fuzzy verification asked
2,048 tasks for the same 17 MiB pickle simultaneously and lost tasks to
EndpointConnectionError against marin-us-east-02a.cwlota.com.

The read had no retry of any kind, so a single refused connection killed the
task, and the coordinator requeued it straight back into the same herd -- the
crash loop that follows is self-sustaining rather than a symptom of bad data.

Retry with a wider spread than an ordinary read: eight attempts backing off to
30 seconds, because a task that waits is also load the next attempt no longer
has to fight.

commit.message:
[zephyr] Reuse the pyarrow filesystem instead of building one per file

_pyarrow_filesystem constructed a fresh S3FileSystem on every call, and it is
called once per file written. Each one carries its own connection pool that
dies with the file, so every request burns an ephemeral port that then sits in
TIME_WAIT for a minute.

Measured on a worker mid-run: 27,612 sockets in TIME_WAIT against a
55,296-port range, 85% of every socket on the box, with tcp_tw_reuse set to 2
and unable to recycle any of them. connect() then fails locally with
EADDRNOTAVAIL in under ten milliseconds, which s3fs, Polars object_store and
pyarrow each report in their own dialect. No retry can help: the connection
never leaves the machine.

Cache one filesystem per process. pyarrow filesystems are thread-safe, so a
single instance serves every task in the process and its pool is reused.

commit.message:
[datakit] Point the store at the 0.75 cluster-text verification

Sampling the 0.60 and 0.75 markers put the choice at 2.09 points of the
corpus: 15.45% removed against 13.36%, and the band between them is only
13.5% of what 0.60 takes. Reading that band is what decides it. Of 17
sampled removals roughly 11 were real duplicates, but four were not, and
they share a failure mode -- a document whose content is one unbroken
token contributes almost no word 3-grams, so two unrelated DNA sequences
score 0.667 through their shared header alone. That contamination is
concentrated where it would be predicted: the marginal band is 4.40pp of
the fact_seeking template QA and 2.47pp of the DNA source against 1.60pp
of ordinary prose.

Per quality bucket the two rules behave the same, so the threshold does
not skew composition -- removals fall monotonically from 20.42% of q0 to
11.30% of q4 at 0.60, and the gap to 0.75 is a flat 1.5 to 1.8 points
across every bucket.

The tree carries 2,383,398,926 markers over all 292 sources. Preflight
passes, which is the first time its layout and coverage checks have run
against a complete artifact.

commit.message:
[datakit] Add the tooling this dedup investigation needed

sample_verified_duplicates.py reads the markers a run actually wrote and
pairs each deleted document with the one kept in its place, so a rule is
judged on its decisions rather than on a recomputation. It streams the
join in small batches because a grouped text partition reaches 8 GiB and
one of its row groups does not fit in a laptop.

reduce_saved_scatter.py rebuilds the reduce from a scatter tree copied
out of the TTL prefix. Zephyr deletes a run's scatter when a pipeline
aborts, so a reduce failure cost the whole map stage -- two hours, three
times. There is no resume inside Zephyr for this, because the scatter
path derives from an execution id minted at run time.

dedup_drop_by_quality.py measures removals per quality bucket using the
store's own calibration. It takes --restrict-to because a missing marker
file means "no duplicates", so comparing two trees of unequal
completeness measures how far each run got rather than what its rule
does.

commit.message:
[datakit] Count the verified drop rate instead of sampling it

Every drop-rate number in this investigation came from a shard sample
against partial marker trees, which forced a restriction to shards both
runs finished and left the absolute rate softer than the ratio between
thresholds. The 0.75 tree is complete, so it can be counted: Parquet
carries row counts in its footer, and the whole corpus costs one
metadata read per file rather than a scan.

Reports three denominators, because the same tree gives three
different-looking answers and all of them are correct -- share of the
normalized corpus, share of the clustered members the rule can act on at
all, and per source, which is what actually moves the mixture.

commit.message:
[datakit] Compare two duplicate rules per store bucket

A corpus-wide drop rate cannot say whether a rule change is safe. The
store partitions on (domain cluster, quality) and mixture weights are set
per bucket, so a rule taking 15% evenly produces a different corpus from
one taking 15% concentrated where the mixture leans.

Buckets are computed the way the store computes them: the domain cluster
from the assignment artifact, and the quality bucket by cutting the score
with the calibration for that document content type rather than the
content-blind default. Both trees are measured over the same shards in
one pass, so a difference between them is a difference in the rules and
not in coverage -- the trap that made the first per-quality run report
0.60 removing less than 0.75.

Attribute directories are resolved through each artifact rather than
assumed, because the pipeline verifier and the cluster-text verifier key
the focus crawl differently.

commit.message:
[datakit] Keep sixteen sources out of fuzzy dedup

The containment rule reads whatever a document has most of. Where that is
a fixed template or a single unbroken token it scores the shared
scaffolding and never sees what distinguishes two records, so a generated
corpus clusters almost entirely and is then read as duplicated:
massive_function_calling loses 94.45% of its documents and every one of
them falls into some cluster, swe-rebench-contree loses 52.56% at 97.4%
clustered.

Exempt sources keep every document the fuzzy rule would have taken.
Contamination and exact duplicates still apply, so byte-identical records
are still dropped whatever their tokenization.

The list carries measured rates per source rather than a rationale, and it
enters the store's hash_attrs, so changing it moves the store rather than
serving a cache built under a different policy. Names are registry names,
which differ from the source keys in ways that are easy to get wrong --
the normalized keys carry a nemotron_pretraining_ prefix the registry
drops, and the legal family is nemotron_legal against
nemotron_pretraining_legal_v1 in its keys -- so build_store_step raises on
a name the registry does not know rather than silently deduplicating a
source the list meant to protect.

commit.message:
[datakit] Sample only the removals the store actually makes

The sampler read every marker in a tree, but the store keeps every
document in an exempt source, so a report drawn from the raw markers
shows pairs that will never be deleted. --exclude-exempt skips them.

The exemption is keyed by registry name and the manifest by source key,
and the two differ by more than a prefix, so the mapping resolves through
each tokenize artifact rather than by string surgery.
